objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly and explain standard rate turns to headings solely by reference to instruments within the CFI ACS limits, and teach a learner the instruments, numbers, cross-check and error fixes behind them.
why: Turns are where a pilot without a horizon most often loses control, and they are also where scan faults show up first. An instructor who can read a learner's turn, name the fault and fix the cause turns hood time into real skill. This Task also carries the compass and timed turns your learners will need when an instrument fails.

warmup: Think first: your learner flies a smooth standard rate turn under the hood, but every turn ends about 100 feet high and 10 degrees past the heading. Before you say a word, what would you watch on the next turn to find out why: which instruments, their eyes, or their hands?

key_terms.def: A turn of 3 degrees per second, a full 360 degrees in 2 minutes [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
The instrument that gives the most pertinent information for pitch, bank or power at that moment of the maneuver; it is usually the one held at a constant reading [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
An instrument that helps keep the primary instrument at its desired reading, such as the attitude indicator while the turn coordinator is primary for bank [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
The continuous, logical observation of instruments for attitude and performance information; also called scanning [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
The second fundamental skill: knowing how each instrument works and what its readings mean for this airplane, maneuver and condition [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
Staring at a single instrument, such as the heading indicator all the way through a turn [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
Leaving an instrument out of the cross-check, such as the heading indicator after a rollout or the slip/skid indicator on a glass panel [[23:146|IFH 6-13]] [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].
Relying on one instrument, usually the one most readily understood, instead of the combination needed [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
Starting the rollout before the desired heading, about half the bank angle as a starting rule [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
A turn using the clock and the turn coordinator to change heading a set number of degrees in a set time [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
In turns the magnetic compass lags on northerly headings and leads on southerly ones, by about the latitude with 15 to 18 degrees of bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
A glass panel line on the heading display that shows the heading 6 seconds ahead; tick marks show half standard and standard rate [[23:159|IFH 6-26]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

chunks.title: The CFI standard and what this lesson adds

body.p: On the CFI practical test you demonstrate and simultaneously explain this Task solely by reference to instruments (ACS AI.XI.D Skills and Objective). The examiner must select at least one Task from Area XI (ACS Area XI note). The S1 standard reads: "Turns to headings, maintain altitude ±100 feet, maintain a standard rate turn, roll out on the assigned heading ±10°, and maintain airspeed ±10 knots." (ACS AI.XI.D.S1)

body.p: A standard rate turn is 3 degrees per second, a full circle in 2 minutes, and it needs more bank as airspeed goes up [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. The IFH wants turns to a specific heading made at standard rate: it gives a timely heading change and still leaves time to cross-check and avoid drastic changes in the aerodynamic forces. At no time should the airplane be maneuvered faster than the pilot can comfortably cross-check, and most autopilots turn at standard rate [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

The AFH does not teach basic attitude instrument flying. It sends pilots and flight instructors to the IFH for these tasks and to the ACS for how they are evaluated [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. So the technique here comes from IFH chapters 6 and 7, and the teaching method from the AIH.

callout.text: Already covered elsewhere: PA.VIII.D (the Private lesson) walks through a turn step by step with the basic bank and lead examples, and AI.VIII.B covers visual level turns. AI.XI.A to C cover straight-and-level, climbs and descents on instruments. This lesson adds the instructor's view: why each rule works, compass and timed turns, teaching under the view-limiting device, and reading a learner's errors.

check.q: What altitude limit will the examiner hold you to, and how does it compare with what your private learners must meet?
check.a: ±100 feet (ACS AI.XI.D.S1), half the ±200 feet private standard (ACS PA.VIII.D.S1). Standard rate, heading ±10° and airspeed ±10 knots are the same in both.

chunks.title: Bank instruments: function, operation and attitude indication

body.p: Attitude is the relationship of the airplane's pitch and roll axes to the earth's horizon. Control instruments show attitude and power directly; performance instruments (altimeter, airspeed indicator, VSI) show what the airplane is actually doing [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]. The method: set an attitude on the control instruments, trim, cross-check the performance instruments, and adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]. The bank instruments are the attitude indicator, heading indicator, magnetic compass and turn coordinator or turn-and-slip indicator [[23:140|IFH 6-7]].
Function and operation, and indication of the aircraft attitude, instrument by instrument:

head: Instrument
Function and operation
Indication of the aircraft attitude in a turn
rows: Attitude indicator
A gyro with a vertical spin axis in a double gimbal; the airplane rolls and pitches around it. Bank lines at 10°, 20°, 30°, 45° and 60° [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]

The only instrument that shows actual attitude both instantly and directly [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]. Read direction of bank from the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar; some bank scales move opposite to the bank, so use the scale only for the amount [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]
Heading indicator
A gyro with a horizontal spin axis; not north seeking, so it is set to the magnetic compass [[23:114|IFH 5-19]] [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]

Supplies the pertinent bank and heading information and is a primary instrument for bank [[23:140|IFH 6-7]], primary again once the wings are level [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; in the turn it tells how far is left to the lead point
Turn coordinator
A rate gyro whose gimbal is canted up about 30°, so it senses both roll and yaw [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]

Shows rate of roll first, then rate of turn once the roll stops [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]. It shows rate and direction of turn, not a bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]], and gives no pitch information [[23:117|IFH 5-22]]
Turn-and-slip indicator
Senses rotation about the vertical axis only [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]
Turn rate only [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]. On a 2 MIN instrument one needle width is standard rate; on a 4 MIN instrument it takes two widths [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]
Inclinometer (ball)
A ball in a curved, liquid-filled tube, moved by gravity and the inertia of the turn [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Shows neither bank nor slip by itself, only the relationship between bank angle and rate of yaw [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]
Magnetic compass
Magnets on a float in fluid; the float can tilt to about 18° of bank [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]
A bank instrument only when used with the heading indicator; it leads and lags in turns [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]

body.p: Glass panels: the turn rate trend vector on the HSI shows where the heading will be in 6 seconds. The first tick mark on each side of the lubber line is half standard rate and the second is standard rate; a vector past the second mark means faster than standard [[23:159|IFH 6-26]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]. The turn rate indicator is the only instrument that can show a standard rate turn exactly, so it is primary for bank in the turn [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

callout.text: Application of IFH 6-2 and 6-3: give the learner one sentence to hang everything on. "The attitude indicator is where you put the airplane. The turn coordinator, heading indicator and altimeter tell you whether it went where you wanted."

check.q: A learner says, "The turn coordinator shows a 20 degree bank." What is wrong with that?
check.a: The turn coordinator shows rate and direction of turn (and roll rate while rolling), not a bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]] [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]. Bank angle is read on the attitude indicator's bank scale [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

chunks.title: Instrument limitations and potential errors in turns

body.p: Instrument limitations and potential errors: every bank instrument can mislead in a turn. Instrument interpretation begins with understanding how each instrument is built and how it works, then applying that to the airplane, the maneuver and the conditions [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

head: Instrument
Limitation or potential error
How the learner catches it
rows: Attitude indicator

A small bank and pitch error is possible after a 180° turn; it corrects itself within a minute or so of straight-and-level flight [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. Some units have bank limits of 100° to 110° and pitch limits of 60° to 70° and can tumble beyond them [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]
After rollout, if the heading keeps changing with wings level and the ball centered, the attitude gyro has precessed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Heading indicator
The earth turns 15° per hour, so it can show up to that much error per hour; worn or dirty bearings add more drift [[1:222|PHAK 8-20]]
Compare it with the magnetic compass at least every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Turn coordinator
The standard rate mark may not give exactly 3° per second [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Once the roll rate is zero it shows only direction and rate of turn [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Calibrate it in each direction; unless the ball is centered, do not assume the turn comes from a bank [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Magnetic compass

Erratic beyond about 18° of bank [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]; affected by acceleration, deceleration, turbulence, climbs, descents and power changes, and leads or lags depending on the turn direction [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
Read it only after returning to straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Vacuum-driven gyros
Low suction makes the attitude and heading indicators unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]; slowing gyros may wander and show a turn that is not happening [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]
Compare the attitude indicator with the turn coordinator and VSI, which use other power sources, and watch the suction gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]
Glass turn rate trend vector
Shows no more than 24° ahead, which is 4° per second; an arrowhead appears past 25° in 6 seconds [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]. It is not shown if part of the system fails [[23:159|IFH 6-26]]
Use it with the primary and supporting instruments, never alone [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]

body.p: Calibrating the turn coordinator: hold the standard rate indication and note the heading at 10 second intervals as the second hand passes a cardinal point. A true standard rate turn changes 30° in 10 seconds. Do it in each direction and use the corrected deflections in all timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. On a glass panel, time the turn between two cardinal headings: 90° of heading change should take 30 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

callout.text: Application: calibrate in VMC on the first instrument turn lesson, with the learner reading the clock. It teaches interpretation as well as numbers: a mark on a dial is a claim to be checked, not a fact.

check.q: Why should a learner compare the attitude indicator with the turn coordinator and VSI when an indication looks wrong?
check.a: They are driven by different systems (vacuum or pressure, electrical, static), so the comparison shows which one has failed [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Most airplanes have two power sources so that some bank information survives a failure [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

body.p: Proper instrument cross-check techniques: cross-check and interpretation are the two fundamental skills. They are learned separately and in deliberate sequence, and precision comes from blending them into smooth, positive control [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. No single scan pattern is required; use the instruments that give the most pertinent information for that phase of the maneuver [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

head: Phase

Pitch and power
What the scan must catch
rows: Roll-in
Attitude indicator, to set the approximate bank [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator as vertical lift drops; airspeed indicator primary for power at constant airspeed [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Pitch, checked as soon as bank pressure starts [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]

Altimeter primary for pitch; airspeed primary for power [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]

Roll-out
Attitude indicator [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Pitch lowered as bank comes off, to arrive at level pitch at zero bank [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]

Heading indicator, as in straight-and-level [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Pitch, power and trim adjusted as lift and airspeed change [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]

bullets: Radial cross-check: 80 to 90 percent of the time on the attitude indicator, with quick glances out to the other instruments and back [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]. On a glass panel a modified radial scan works well in turns [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].
Rectangular cross-check: gives every instrument equal weight, but lengthens the time to get back to the instrument that matters most for the maneuver [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].
Inverted-V: taught in PA.VIII.D; it pairs the turn coordinator and VSI around the attitude indicator [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].
A beginner may scan fast without knowing what to look for; with experience the pilot learns what to look for, when and what to do, and suits the scan rate to the maneuver [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

body.p: Fixation and omission, with emphasis, the third classic fault, as they show up in turns:

bullets: Fixation: a shallow bank for a 90° turn, then staring at the heading indicator all the way around. There is no need to recheck it for about 25 seconds after entry. The cause may be interpretation (unsure how to read it) or control (inconsistent rollouts) [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. On glass, fixating on the trend vector is common in new pilots [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

Omission: rolling out of a 180° steep turn on the attitude indicator alone and never checking the heading indicator, while the attitude gyro shows a slight precession error [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. On glass, standby instruments, the magnetic compass and especially the slip/skid indicator get left out [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

Emphasis: relying on the instrument most readily understood even when it gives poor information; the attitude indicator alone holds altitude only roughly [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Rolling out of a 180° turn needs the attitude indicator, heading indicator, slip/skid indicator and altimeter together [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

callout.text: Spotting it from the right seat: glance at the learner's eyes. A gaze held on one instrument suggests fixation; a gaze that never reaches the engine gauges suggests inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Fixation often means the task has not had enough practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

check.q: A learner holds standard rate well, but every turn entry costs about 100 feet. Which cross-check fault fits, and what do you have them change?
check.a: Emphasis on bank (preoccupation with bank control on entry) at the cost of pitch [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Have them check the pitch instruments as soon as bank pressure starts and control the total attitude, not one factor at a time [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

chunks.title: The numbers: bank angle, small turns and lead

body.p: The IFH rule of thumb for standard rate bank is 15 percent of true airspeed: divide the airspeed by 10 and add half the result [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. The PHAK gives the physics behind it: rate of turn in degrees per second equals 1,091 times the tangent of the bank angle, divided by true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. Application: solving that for 3 degrees per second shows how close the rule is.

head: True airspeed
Rule: TAS ÷ 10 + half
Bank for exactly 3°/s (PHAK formula)
rows: 90 knots
120 knots
160 knots

body.p: Because the bank for a given rate of turn depends on true airspeed, the bank must change in proportion to any airspeed change. When slowing in a turn, decrease the bank and raise the pitch to hold altitude and standard rate [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Normal standard rate banks run about 10° to 20° [[23:214|IFH 7-53]], and for instrument training any turn faster than standard rate counts as steep [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
Small heading changes. The IFH gives three versions; teach the third for precision and the first two as limits:

bullets: Bank angle normally approximates the degrees to turn, not to exceed 30° [[23:137|IFH 6-4]].
For small heading changes, use a bank that does not exceed the number of degrees to be turned [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Better defined: about half the heading change, but never more than standard rate [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

body.p: Lead the heading by about half the bank angle. The real lead depends on rate of turn, bank and rate of recovery, so practice with half the bank until the lead for the learner's own technique is known; consistent roll-in and roll-out rates make it repeatable [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Strive for the same rate of roll-out as roll-in [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. On glass, the turn rate indicator sits on the compass rose, which helps judge when to start the rollout [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

callout.text: Speed ÷ 10, plus half = bank. Half the bank = lead. Small turn: half the change, never past standard rate.

check.q: Why does a 160 knot airplane need a steeper bank than a 100 knot trainer for the same standard rate turn?
check.a: Rate of turn = 1,091 x tan(bank) / TAS, so at a higher TAS the bank must grow to keep 3° per second [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. The IFH says the bank for a given rate is proportional to true airspeed [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

chunks.title: Timed turns and magnetic compass turns

body.p: Timed turns use the clock and the turn coordinator: at standard rate the airplane turns 45° in 15 seconds; at half standard rate, 45° in 30 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The cross-check is the same as for turns to headings, with the clock in place of the heading indicator: turn coordinator primary for bank, altimeter for pitch, airspeed indicator for power. Start the roll-in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, hold the calibrated standard rate (or half standard rate for small changes), and roll out when the computed seconds are up. If roll-in and roll-out rates match, they need not be counted [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

bullets: Practice timed turns with a full panel first and check accuracy on the heading indicator. Without it, check the turn on the magnetic compass afterward, allowing for compass deviation [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

On a glass panel, after an AHRS or magnetometer failure, timed turns are used instead of compass turns because they are simpler: they do not require accounting for the compass errors [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

body.p: Compass turns. In most small airplanes the magnetic compass is the only direction instrument independent of other instruments and power sources, and knowing its errors lets a pilot turn to and hold headings with it [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The IFH points [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]:

bullets: On north, starting a turn east or west: the compass lags, or at first shows a turn the other way.
On south, starting a turn east or west: the compass leads, showing more turn than is happening.
On east or west: the compass reads correctly when a turn starts in either direction.
On east or west: acceleration shows a turn toward north; deceleration shows a turn toward south.
Holding north or south: no error from diving, climbing or changing airspeed.

body.p: With 15° to 18° of bank, the lead or lag for northerly and southerly headings is about equal to the latitude. Turning to north, the rollout lead is the latitude plus the normal rollout lead. Turning to south, keep turning until the compass passes south by the latitude, minus the normal lead. At 30° latitude with 15° of bank: east to north, start the rollout at 037°; east to south, at 203°; from the west, at 323° and 157°. Turning to east or west, start the rollout about 10° to 12° early from a northerly heading and about 5° early from a southerly heading [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

Errors during compass turns: faulty understanding or computation of lead and lag, and fixation on the compass during the rollout. Until the airplane is straight, level and unaccelerated the reading means little, so cross-check for straight-and-level first, then check the heading [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Abrupt attitude or airspeed changes make the card move erratically [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

callout.text: The sources disagree on the compass lead. The PHAK rule of thumb stops a northerly turn 15° plus half the latitude early and a southerly turn the same amount late [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. The IFH uses the latitude plus the normal rollout lead [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. On a turn to north at 40° latitude they differ by 12.5°. Teach the IFH method for instrument turns and treat either result as an estimate to check once the wings are level.

check.q: At 30° north, a learner turning left from east to north with 15° of bank starts the rollout as the compass passes N. What happens, and why?
check.a: They overshoot well past north. Turning to north the compass lags, so the IFH starts the rollout at about 037°: 30° of latitude plus half the 15° bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

chunks.title: Control application and trimming the aircraft

body.p: Control application solely by reference to instruments: pilots commonly roll into turns much too fast. In early training, base control pressures on the rate of cross-check and interpretation; maneuvering faster than the scan can follow only creates corrections [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

bullets: Grip: a tight grip makes it hard to feel pressure changes, and relaxing takes conscious effort early in instrument training [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]. The IFH calls an excessively strong grip "tension" [[23:363|IFH G-18]].
Pitch on the attitude indicator: corrections of no more than half a bar width at a time [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].
Roll-in: as the vertical component of lift drops, add aft pressure enough to stop any altitude loss trend, then power for the extra drag [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].
Some airplanes are very stable in turns; others need constant, rapid cross-check to stop an overbanking tendency [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Know which one you teach in.
Roll-out: decrease pitch as the bank decreases so the airplane reaches level pitch at zero bank [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

body.p: Trimming the aircraft: trim off the pressures from pitch and power changes as the bank is established, and check the ball throughout, especially if pressures are held instead of trimmed off [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Unless the airplane is trimmed, the pilot cannot tell whether a pressure change comes from aerodynamics or from their own hands [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Trim alone used to change attitude usually gives erratic control; control pressure first, then trim [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. Poor trim is one of the most common errors instructors note in instrument students [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

callout.text: Application of IFH 7-3: after the rollout, if you see white knuckles, have the learner trim for level flight and briefly release the elevator pressure. The airplane is stable and holds level flight if left alone in smooth air, which teaches more than any words.

check.q: Why tie a learner's roll-in rate to their cross-check instead of to a fixed number of seconds?
check.a: Maneuvering faster than the learner can keep up with the instrument changes only creates the need for corrections, so the IFH bases control pressures on the rate of cross-check and interpretation [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

body.p: Loss of control in an instrument turn usually starts with an overbank. Overbanking without adjusting pitch needs ever stronger elevator pressure, and the loss of vertical lift and rise in wing loading reach a point where more back pressure tightens the turn without raising the nose [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

Instrument interpretation: a rapid downward movement of the altimeter and VSI together with rising airspeed, despite back pressure, means a diving spiral [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Recovery [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]:

bullets: Shallow the bank at once with smooth, coordinated aileron and rudder, holding or slightly relaxing the elevator pressure.
Speed up the cross-check of the attitude indicator, altimeter and VSI; reduce power if airspeed is rising fast.
As the vertical speed trends upward and the elevator becomes effective, hold the bank shown on the attitude indicator and set the nose-high attitude that bank needs.

body.p: If a learner's pitch control is consistently late on steep entries, roll out, analyze the errors, and go back to shallower turns before increasing the bank [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Prolonged turns also invite progressive overbanking [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

callout.text: Application: teach the spiral as a picture to recognize before it is a procedure. Have the learner name it out loud ("spiral: shallow the bank") before touching the elevator, since pulling first is the instinct that tightens it.

check.q: In a diving spiral, why shallow the bank before raising the nose?
check.a: In a steep bank with little vertical lift, more back pressure tightens the turn without raising the nose; shallowing the bank restores vertical lift so the elevator can work [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

chunks.title: Instrument flying hazards: disorientation, VFR into IMC and afterward

body.p: Spatial disorientation in turns: the fluid in the semicircular canals takes about 15 to 20 seconds to catch up with a turn [[23:71|IFH 3-4]]. A steady turn then feels like no turn, and the rollout feels like a turn the other way, so the pilot may roll back into the original turn [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. In a long turn with an unnoticed altitude loss, pulling back tightens the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Skids and slips feel like banking, and fatigue or illness make these sensations worse [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

Teach it with the IFH demonstrations. Their aims: show how susceptible the body is, show that attitude judged by feel is often wrong, reduce disorientation through understanding, and build trust in the instruments. Even no sensation at all is a useful demo, because it shows the body cannot detect the bank [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. Never fly them at low altitude or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

head: IFH demonstration (turn related)
How it is flown
Usual illusion
rows: Climbing while turning
Learner's eyes closed; slow entry to a coordinated turn of about 1.5 G (about 50° bank) for 90°
A climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]

Same, with eyes kept closed until the recovery is about half done
Tilting to right or left
Wings level with a slight skid
Body tilted the other way [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]
Reversal of motion
A smooth, positive roll to about 45°
Strong rotation in the opposite direction [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]
Diving or rolling beyond the vertical plane
Roll toward 30° to 40° of bank while the learner tilts the head forward, looks left or right, then sits up
Intense: falling into the roll [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]

body.p: Failure to maintain VFR: pilots without instrument training, or whose skills have eroded, lose control in about 10 minutes once forced onto the instruments [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Turns are perhaps the most dangerous maneuver for them, so the AFH limits them to the smallest practical bank, never more than 10°, turning a few degrees, leveling and repeating [[24:368|AFH 18-19]]. Tell every learner that hood work does not prepare them for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

bullets: Loss of control: the tendency to overcontrol leads to steep banks and a possible graveyard spiral [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

Fatigue: illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia increase susceptibility to disorientation, so be rested and physically tuned before flying in reduced visibility [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

Stress: the body's response to demands placed on it [[23:363|IFH G-18]]. In IMC the pilot must not panic and should make a conscious effort to relax [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]; under overload, people tend to lower their standards [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

Emergency off airport landings: after an IMC encounter, the pilot may break out with poor visibility, over unfamiliar terrain, too low for a normal pattern, and under self-induced pressure to land. If possible, take time to become acclimatized and oriented first, even flying straight and level or circling [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. A ballistic parachute, if installed and deployed within an acceptable flight regime, is another option [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

check.q: During a disorientation demo, your learner feels nothing at all. Was the demo wasted?
check.a: No. The absence of sensation is itself the lesson: it shows the body cannot detect the bank or roll [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

chunks.title: Getting help, collision hazards and distractions

body.p: When to seek assistance or declare an emergency in a deteriorating situation: an aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else that could affect safety, and that is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. With an instrument failure, advise ATC and, if necessary, declare an emergency before the situation deteriorates beyond the pilot's ability to recover [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. When ATC sounds urgent with heading changes, do not rush into a maneuver that could cause loss of control; asking the controller to slow down is reasonable [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

Collision hazards: the learner under the hood cannot look out. The safety pilot must have adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer must supplement it [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. Instructors and safety pilots should guard against preoccupation and be especially alert during simulated instrument flight, where there is a tendency to look inside too much [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]. In one study of midair collisions, flight instructors were on board in 37 percent, and most collisions happened in VFR daylight [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

bullets: Distractions: AIH examples that suit hood turns include resetting the clock, finding a heading to an airport on a chart and computing true airspeed [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

Task prioritization: before stacking tasks, make sure each can be done reasonably well on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. In a demanding turn, attend to the most important tasks first; holding pitch constant frees time for the cross-check [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].
Loss of situational awareness: forgetting the heading being turned to is likely when rushing [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; a heading bug is a visible reminder [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].
Disorientation: a head movement during a long turn can trigger the Coriolis illusion; pick up dropped items with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

callout.text: Application: interruptions are where steps get skipped [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. If you hand the learner a distraction mid-turn, watch whether they still start the rollout at the lead point afterward.

check.q: Your learner is in a long standard rate turn when you ask them to pick up a dropped pencil. What risk are you creating, and how should they do it?
check.a: A head movement during a prolonged turn can cause the Coriolis illusion; retrieve it with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Application: better yet, give that distraction in straight flight.

body.p: Instrument references belong in every maneuver from the first time it is introduced, with no difference in how the controls are used [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Your learner has already flown visual turns (AI.VIII.B) and private-level hood turns (PA.VIII.D), so build from the known [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Before the flight, brief which instrument is primary in each phase (chunk 4), the standard rate bank and lead for the training airplane's true airspeed, and the roll-in rule: no faster than the scan [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

head: Step (application, built on the IFH and AIH)
What it teaches
Source
rows: 1. In VMC, calibrate the turn coordinator both ways and note the bank at standard rate
Interpretation; the airplane's own numbers
2. Demonstrate a standard rate turn to a heading under the hood, flying it in the same order you explained it
A correct first picture
3. Learner talks you through the next turn: primary instrument, bank, lead
Shows whether the learner understands before flying it
4. Learner flies left and right turns with consistent roll rates
A repeatable lead
5. Add small heading changes, timed turns, then compass turns
Bank for small changes; flying with failed instruments
6. Add airspeed changes in turns, then distractions
All three basic skills at once

body.p: Teaching under a view-limiting device:

bullets: The rules: the other control seat holds a safety pilot with at least a private certificate for the category and class [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], with adequate vision to the front and sides [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]], in an airplane with fully functioning dual controls. A single throwover wheel is allowed in a single-engine airplane only when the safety pilot finds it safe and the pilot flying holds at least a private certificate with the category and class [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]].
Keep your own eyes outside; simulated instrument flight pulls instructors inside [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].
Have the learner set the heading bug on every assigned heading [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].
Safety permitting, let the learner go part way into a mistake, such as missing the lead, and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
If the turns look good, change one thing (airspeed, a climb, a compass turn) to check that the learner understands rather than imitates [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
Listen while the learner flies and talks: you can tell a misconception from a motor skill problem [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Application: the hood takes away the learner's lookout, not yours. The regulation puts the vision requirement on the safety pilot [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]], and in this airplane that is you.

check.q: Why practice timed turns with the full panel before covering the heading indicator?
check.a: So the heading indicator can check the accuracy of each timed turn; without it, the compass is used after the turn, allowing for deviation [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

body.p: The IFH lists the common errors in turns under pitch, bank, power and trim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]], and adds glass panel errors [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]. For S2 the examiner will fly some of them. Name what you see, say the cause, and give one fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Preoccupation with bank on entry
Altitude sags during the roll-in
Check pitch as bank pressure starts; control the total attitude [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Forgetting the vertical lift change
Consistent altitude loss on every entry
Explain why, then add pitch as the bank goes in [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Premature or overcontrolled back pressure
Nose rises early; pitch hunts; often with a slow scan and fast entry [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Slow the roll-in to the scan [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Not lowering pitch on rollout
Consistent altitude gain after each turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Lower pitch as the bank decreases [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]
No straight-and-level cross-check after rollout
A perfect turn, then drift [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Keep the scan running after wings level
Overcontrolling bank
Overbanks on entry; overshoots and undershoots headings [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Smaller pressures; set bank on the attitude indicator, then hold standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Fixation on one bank instrument
Eyes parked on the heading indicator [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Leave it out about 20 seconds in a 90° turn; check what needs checking [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Too much bank for the change
A 20° bank for a 10° change overshoots [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Bank to suit the change [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]
Forgetting the heading or turning the wrong way
Hesitation, or a turn the long way [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Heading bug; visualize the eight major compass points [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Not checking the ball
Turn coordinator shows a turn while the ball is off center [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Do not assume bank causes the turn unless the ball is centered [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Power errors
Airspeed drifts; throttle moved repeatedly; poor friction setting [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Cross-check airspeed as pitch changes; set power, then recheck its effect [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Trim errors
Tension on the controls; chasing the VSI [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Trim after entry, after power changes and after a long turn's rollout [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Glass: cannot hold the bank for standard rate
Turn rate trend wanders past or short of the mark [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]
An aggressive cross-check of the bank against the turn rate indicator [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]
Glass: fixation on the turn rate indicator
Altitude and airspeed drift while the trend sits perfect [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]
A modified radial scan [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]

body.p: Errors in turns are more exaggerated, harder to correct and harder to analyze unless the rates of entry and recovery suit the learner's proficiency [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Application: slow everything down first, then name one error at a time, starting with the scan.

callout.text: Application: fix the cause, not the number. "You lost 80 feet" helps less than "your eyes stayed on the heading indicator while the bank went in."

check.q: The examiner, playing your learner, rolls into each turn in about 2 seconds and then hunts pitch for the rest of the turn. Name it and give your fix.
check.a: Overcontrolled, premature back pressure from an entry too fast for the cross-check [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Slow the roll-in to what the scan can follow [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

scenario.title: First hood turns with a commercial applicant
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Your learner, a private pilot working toward a commercial certificate, is under the hood at 4,500 feet in a trainer cruising at 110 knots true, near 41° north latitude. The haze is thick but the weather is VFR. You plan turns to headings, then a covered heading indicator and compass turns.

questions.q: What bank and lead should the learner plan for a standard rate turn?
questions.a: About 16.5° of bank (110 ÷ 10 = 11, plus half = 5.5) [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], and a rollout lead of about half that, roughly 8° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

questions.q: On a 90° turn, the learner's eyes stay on the heading indicator and the altitude drifts down. What is happening and what do you say?
questions.a: Fixation: there is no need to recheck the heading indicator for about 25 seconds after entry [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Their fixed gaze is the clue [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Coach the pitch check as the bank goes in [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

questions.q: You cover the heading indicator. The learner is on east and you assign a left turn to north. When should they start the rollout on the compass?
questions.a: At about 049°: lag equal to the latitude (41°) plus the normal lead (half of 16.5°, about 8°) [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Then level the wings and read the compass only once straight and unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

questions.q: While you check the learner's compass math, a target appears on the traffic display. Whose job is the lookout?
questions.a: Yours as the safety pilot: you must have adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]], and instructors must guard against preoccupation during simulated instrument flight [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

questions.q: After a long turn the learner says, "We're turning right," but the attitude indicator shows wings level. What do you tell them?
questions.a: The rollout sends the inner-ear fluid the other way and creates a false sense of turning; pilots may roll back into the turn. Believe the instruments [[23:72|IFH 3-5]] [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

questions.q: The haze thickens and you are no longer sure you can stay VFR back to the airport. When should you ask for help?
questions.a: Now. The moment you are doubtful about weather you are in at least an urgency condition, and that is the time to ask [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Take off the hood and fly; if ATC gives quick vectors, do not let urgency rush a maneuver [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

skills.do: Turns to headings, maintain altitude ±100 feet, maintain a standard rate turn, roll out on the assigned heading ±10°, and maintain airspeed ±10 knots (ACS AI.XI.D.S1), solely by reference to instruments while simultaneously explaining. In plain words: hold altitude within 100 feet, keep the turn at 3° per second, finish within 10° of the heading and within 10 knots, while saying which instrument is primary, what bank and lead you chose, and why.
skills.practice: With a safety pilot, fly left and right turns of 30°, 90° and 180° while talking: call the bank (TAS ÷ 10 plus half) [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], the lead, and the primary instrument at each phase [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Add a timed turn and a compass turn each flight [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], and log your altitude error on every rollout.

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task (ACS AI.XI.D.S2): watch the examiner fly flawed instrument turns, name each error from the IFH list, give the likely cause (often the cross-check), and coach one specific fix, taking the controls if safety requires.
skills.practice: Have another applicant fly the IFH pitch, bank, power and trim errors on purpose [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] while you watch their eyes and the panel [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]; diagnose aloud within one turn and coach the fix in one sentence.

quiz.q: Why does the IFH want turns to a specific heading made at standard rate?
options: It keeps the load factor low enough that stall speed in the turn does not change
It keeps the magnetic compass inside its tilt limit all the way around
It gives a timely heading change while leaving time to cross-check and avoid drastic force changes
It matches the roll rate an attitude gyro can follow without precessing during the entry
quiz.why: Standard rate gives a timely heading change and leaves time to cross-check and avoid drastic changes in aerodynamic forces [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

quiz.q: Which instrument shows rate of roll first and then rate of turn once the roll stops?
options: Turn coordinator
Turn-and-slip indicator
Heading indicator
Magnetic compass
quiz.why: Its canted gimbal senses roll and yaw, so it shows bank rate first and then turn rate once stabilized [[23:141|IFH 6-8]] [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: A turn-and-slip indicator in a faster airplane is marked "4 MIN TURN." Where is standard rate?
options: One needle width either side of center
Half a needle width either side of center
Four needle widths either side of center
Two needle widths either side of center
quiz.why: On a 2 MIN instrument one needle width is 3° per second; on a 4 MIN instrument the same rate takes two widths [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: On a glass panel trainer, an arrowhead appears on the end of your learner's turn rate trend vector. What does the IFH say it means?
options: The AHRS has failed, and the vector is frozen at its last turn rate
The turn rate is past 25° in 6 seconds, beyond what the vector can show
The turn is at exactly standard rate, so the bank should be held right there
The heading bug is set more than 24° away from the current heading
quiz.why: The vector shows no more than 24° ahead (4° per second); when the turn passes 25° in 6 seconds an arrowhead is added [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]. A system failure removes the vector rather than freezing it [[23:159|IFH 6-26]].

quiz.q: Using the IFH "half the heading change, never more than standard rate" rule, what bank fits a 10° heading change at 120 knots?
options: About 18°, standard rate
About 5°
About 10°, equal to the change
About 15°, the trainer standard
quiz.why: Half of 10° is 5°, well under the 18° standard rate bank at 120 knots [[23:213|IFH 7-52]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

quiz.q: Your school's trainer has an attitude indicator whose bank pointer moves opposite to the bank. How should your learner tell which way the airplane is banked?
options: From the bank pointer, since it always moves the same way as the wings
From the heading indicator alone, since this attitude indicator cannot show direction
From the ball, which moves toward the low wing in a coordinated turn
From the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar; the scale gives only the amount
quiz.why: Some bank scales move opposite to the bank and can confuse; the PHAK says to read direction of bank from the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]. The ball stays centered in a coordinated turn [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: After an AHRS or magnetometer failure on a glass panel, why does the IFH use timed turns instead of compass turns?
options: They are simpler: there are no compass errors to account for
The compass is unpowered once the AHRS fails
Timed turns are required by the ACS after a failure
The trend vector works without the magnetometer
quiz.why: Compass turns require accounting for the compass errors; timed turns do not, so they are simpler [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

quiz.q: Which does the IFH name as one of the most common errors instructors note in instrument students?
options: Setting the altimeter incorrectly
Reading the bank scale backwards
Poor trim
Overleaning the mixture
quiz.why: Poor trim is one of the most common errors instructors note in instrument students [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

quiz.q: What does the IFH change to turn the climbing while turning demonstration into the diving while turning one?
options: The instructor enters the turn abruptly instead of slowly, at the same bank
The learner keeps the eyes closed until the recovery is about half done
The bank is steepened from about 50° to about 70° to add more G
The learner makes the inputs you call, with the head tilted to one side
quiz.why: Diving while turning repeats the climbing while turning procedure, except the eyes stay closed until the recovery is about half completed; the usual illusion is a dive [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

quiz.q: You give hood instruction in a single-engine airplane with a single throwover control wheel. When does 14 CFR 91.109 allow that?
options: Whenever the instructor holds an instrument instructor rating and logs the flight as dual instruction given to the pilot flying
Only in day VMC with a visible horizon and no passengers
Never; any simulated instrument flight needs fixed dual controls for elevator and ailerons
When the safety pilot finds it safe and the pilot flying holds at least a private certificate for the category and class
quiz.why: In simulated instrument flight the throwover wheel exception needs both conditions [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]]; 91.109(a) sets the same two conditions, with the instructor deciding, for instrument flight instruction [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Partial panel, your learner is on south and turns right to west using only the magnetic compass. When does the IFH say to start the rollout?
options: About 10° to 12° before the compass reads west
After the compass passes west by about the latitude
About 5° before the compass reads west
Exactly as it reads west, since west needs no lead
final_quiz.why: Turning to east or west, start the rollout about 5° early from a southerly heading and about 10° to 12° early from a northerly one [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

final_quiz.q: To finish a partial panel compass turn to north sooner, your learner rolls into 30° of bank. Why do you stop them?
options: The IFH lead and lag figures assume 15° to 18° of bank, and the card turns erratic past about 18°
A steep bank makes the compass lead on northerly headings, so the IFH lag figure reverses
The turn coordinator gyro tumbles past about 20° of bank and leaves no rate reference at all
The CFI ACS requires compass turns at half standard rate, which this bank angle far exceeds
final_quiz.why: The lead or lag is about the latitude only with 15° to 18° of bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], and the compass float tilts only to about 18°, so steeper banks give erratic readings [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: On a glass panel, the learner's turn rate trend vector reaches only the first tick mark. What does that show, and what do you coach for a standard rate turn?
options: Half standard rate; increase the bank until the vector reaches the second mark
Standard rate already; hold that bank and watch the altitude tape
More than 4° per second; shallow the bank until the arrowhead disappears
A trend failure; the vector is unreliable until the AHRS realigns
final_quiz.why: The first tick mark is half standard rate and the second is standard rate [[23:159|IFH 6-26]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner keeps staring at the heading indicator through every 90° turn, even after you point it out. Besides the scan itself, what does the IFH say may be causing it?
options: A heading indicator that has drifted since it was last set
Poor trim, so the learner watches heading to sense the turn
A turn coordinator that was not calibrated before the hood
Uncertainty reading the heading indicator, or inconsistent rollouts
final_quiz.why: The IFH says this fixation may not be entirely a cross-check error: uncertainty about reading the heading indicator (interpretation) or inconsistent rollouts (control) may cause it [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Fix the cause, then have them leave it out for about 20 seconds in a 90° turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: In a standard rate turn at 120 knots, ATC asks you to slow to 90 knots and keep turning. How should bank and pitch change?
options: Increase bank and lower pitch
Hold the bank and raise pitch
Decrease bank, raise pitch
Decrease bank and lower pitch
final_quiz.why: Bank for a given rate is proportional to true airspeed; when slowing, decrease bank and increase pitch to hold altitude and standard rate [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

final_quiz.q: Under the hood, the attitude indicator slowly shows a left bank while the turn coordinator shows wings level and the VSI is steady at zero. What fits the IFH guidance?
options: Follow the attitude indicator; it is the only direct attitude instrument
Suspect a gyro or vacuum failure; cross-check the turn coordinator and VSI
Roll right until the attitude indicator shows level, then retrim and continue the turn
Declare an emergency and descend at once to find VFR below
final_quiz.why: Compare the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI to find the failed system, then use the working instruments [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Low suction makes the gyros unreliable [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

final_quiz.q: You want your learner to experience disorientation while actually flying the airplane. Which IFH version fits?
options: Hood on, the learner flies a 45° bank turn while you cover the attitude indicator
Eyes closed and head tilted, the learner makes the inputs you call, then looks up
Eyes open, the learner rolls briskly to 45° and back while watching a wingtip
Eyes closed, the learner flies a 1.5 G turn alone with no calls from you at all
final_quiz.why: The IFH says having the pilot fly can be very effective: eyes closed and head tilted, the instructor calls the inputs, and once disoriented the pilot is told to look up and recover [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

final_quiz.q: On the roll-in, once the turn coordinator shows standard rate, what does the IFH have the pilot note?
options: The pitch attitude in bar widths above the artificial horizon
The vertical speed reading, to confirm the turn is level
The exact bank angle on the attitude indicator's bank scale
The power setting needed to hold airspeed in the turn
final_quiz.why: Set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, check the turn coordinator for standard rate, then note the exact bank shown on the attitude indicator's banking scale [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Application: that number becomes the learner's bank target in this airplane.

final_quiz.q: You add airspeed changes to your learner's standard rate turns. Which way does the IFH call easier?
options: Start the airspeed change at the same moment as the roll-in
Change the airspeed after the turn is established
Start the airspeed change during the rollout so both end together
Change power just before the roll-in so speed settles in the turn
final_quiz.why: The IFH gives two methods: change airspeed after the turn is established, or start it with the turn entry. The first is easier, and either way the cross-check must speed up as power is reduced [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

final_quiz.q: Partial panel, your learner stares at the compass during the rollout and keeps chasing the swinging card. What do you coach?
options: Roll out faster so the card settles sooner
Read the average of the swings and stop the turn there
Use a steeper bank so the turn ends before the compass card starts to swing
Get straight, level and unaccelerated first, then check the heading
final_quiz.why: Fixation on the compass during the rollout is a listed error; it is unnecessary to read it until straight-and-level unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. The compass is erratic beyond about 18° of bank [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your school switches to a trainer in which every instrument turn slowly steepens unless your learner holds it. What does the IFH say this airplane needs?
options: Only slight trim changes, then hands-off flight once the bank is set
Turns flown at half standard rate so the bank never gets steep
Constant, rapid cross-check and control to correct the overbanking
Rudder held against the turn to keep the bank from growing
final_quiz.why: Some airplanes are very stable in turns and need only slight trim changes; others need constant, rapid cross-check and control to correct overbanking tendencies [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

final_quiz.q: Mid-turn, your learner hesitates and asks what heading they were turning to. When does the IFH say this is likely, and what reminder fits?
options: When rushing the maneuver; have them set the heading bug on each assigned heading
When fatigued late in a lesson; end the hood work for the day and debrief the turns
When the compass swings in the turn; reset the heading indicator before each turn
When the bank is too shallow; use full standard rate for every heading change
final_quiz.why: Failure to remember the heading is likely when rushing the maneuver [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; heading bugs remind the pilot of assigned headings [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner, as your learner, holds strong back pressure through a long standard rate turn and the ball wanders. Which IFH point fits best?
options: Overbanking: shallow the bank before adding any more back pressure
Failure to trim on entry; check the ball when pressures are held
Turn coordinator error: recalibrate the instrument
Fixation on the altimeter: widen the scan to include the VSI and airspeed
final_quiz.why: Trim off pressures as the bank is set and check the ball, especially if pressures are held [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; failure to trim during entry is a listed error [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

takeaways: CFI standard: altitude ±100 feet, standard rate, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots, all while explaining (ACS AI.XI.D.S1).
Attitude indicator sets the bank; turn coordinator is primary once standard rate is set; attitude indicator again on rollout; heading indicator once level.
Bank = TAS ÷ 10 plus half; lead = half the bank; small turns use about half the change, never past standard rate.
Compass turns: lag to north, lead to south, by about the latitude with 15 to 18° of bank; read it only when straight and unaccelerated.
Fixation, omission and emphasis are the scan faults; the learner's eyes show them first.
A diving spiral is fixed by shallowing the bank before raising the nose.
Under the hood, the lookout is the safety pilot's job: yours.
cfi_notes: The IFH gives two times for leaving the heading indicator out of the scan in a 90° turn: about 25 seconds (6-13) and about 20 seconds (7-25). Same point: do not stare at it.

The IFH gives three small-turn bank rules: about the degrees to turn, not over 30° (6-4); not more than the degrees to turn (7-20); about half the change, never more than standard rate (7-52). Teach the last for precision and the others as limits.

Compass lead sources disagree. For a turn to north the IFH uses latitude plus the normal rollout lead (7-22); the PHAK uses 15° plus half the latitude (8-26). At 40° north that is 47.5° against 35°; for a turn to south the gap is only 2.5° (32.5° against 35°). The PHAK also names the errors the other way round (its card "leads" turning north and "lags" turning south), while the IFH says the indication lags toward north and leads toward south. Both stop early for north and late for south. Teach the IFH for instrument compass turns.

The analog calibration wording (IFH 7-21, "more than or less than 30° ... a respectively larger or smaller deflection") reads backward if taken literally. If the airplane turns more than 30° in 10 seconds it is turning faster than standard rate and needs less deflection; check it against the clock rather than the wording. The glass wording (7-53, a deflection above or below the line) is neutral.
Application of PHAK 5-38: the 15 percent rule is within about half a degree of the exact standard rate bank from 90 to 160 knots, so learners can trust it in trainers.
The AFH 10° bank limit (18-19) is for an untrained pilot in an IMC emergency, not the standard for hood training. Make the difference clear so a private learner does not think standard rate is wrong.
IFH 6-28 still refers to the Instrument Rating PTS for airspeed latitude; the point (no need to hold airspeed to 1 knot) still stands.

In the IFH disorientation demonstrations the instructor usually flies with the learner's eyes closed, but the IFH also offers a version where the learner flies, eyes closed and head tilted, following your calls (3-8). Brief either one on the ground and make the exchange of controls clear before you start.

IFH 5-21 says a standard rate turn is made "whenever the needle aligns with a doghouse" in either instrument, then says a 4 MIN instrument needs two needle widths for 3° per second. Teach the needle-width rule with the dial marking, and confirm it with the clock.
gaps: No source gives the power increase needed to hold airspeed in a standard rate turn for a given trainer; the IFH only says to add power as drag increases. Use the POH/AFM and experience.
The compass lead and lag values assume 15° to 18° of bank; no source gives values for other banks, and for other headings the IFH only says to interpolate.
The exact rollout lead depends on the pilot's roll rate; the IFH says to find it by practice, so no fixed number applies to every learner.
No source gives a turn-specific procedure for an emergency off airport landing after IMC; the AFH covers only general orientation and acclimatization.
Beyond AC 90-48E's general advice, no source tells a safety pilot how to divide attention between the learner's panel and the lookout.

activities.title: Work the instrument turn numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: At 40° north with 15° of bank, turning right from west to north on the compass: at what compass heading should the rollout start (IFH method)?
items.why: Lag = latitude 40 plus normal lead 15 / 2 = 7.5, so start 47.5° before north. Turning right, the heading is increasing toward 360: 360 - 47.5 = 312.5° [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The IFH example at 30° gives 323° the same way.

items.q: At 40° north with 15° of bank, how many degrees apart are the rollout points for a turn to north by the IFH method (latitude plus half the bank) and by the PHAK rule (15 plus half the latitude)?
Your calibration shows the standard rate mark turns the airplane 99° in 30 seconds. Holding that same indication, how many seconds for a 90° timed turn?
items.why: Actual rate = 99 / 30 = 3.3° per second; 90 / 3.3 = 27.3 seconds. A true standard rate turn would give 90° in 30 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

items.q: For a 15° heading change by timed turn at half standard rate, how many seconds do you hold the turn?
items.why: Half standard rate = 1.5° per second; 15 / 1.5 = 10 seconds. The IFH uses half standard rate for small changes [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

items.q: On a glass panel in a standard rate turn, how many degrees ahead of the current heading does the turn rate trend vector point?
items.why: The vector shows the heading in 6 seconds: 3° per second x 6 = 18° [[23:159|IFH 6-26]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

items.q: At 120 knots, what bank does the "half the change, never more than standard rate" rule give for a 40° heading change?
items.why: Half the change = 40 / 2 = 20°, but standard rate at 120 knots = 12 + 6 = 18°, which is the limit [[23:213|IFH 7-52]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

activities.title: Recover from the diving spiral
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Recognize it: altimeter and VSI dropping fast and airspeed rising despite back pressure
Shallow the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, holding or slightly relaxing the elevator
Speed up the cross-check of attitude indicator, altimeter and VSI; reduce power if airspeed is rising fast
Watch the vertical speed trend upward as vertical lift returns
Hold the bank on the attitude indicator and set the nose-high attitude that bank needs

activities.title: True or false: disorientation and IMC
activities.intro: Tap True or False for each card.

cards.s: In the IFH tilting demonstration, a slight skid to the left with wings level makes the learner feel tilted to the right.
cards.why: True. A skid to the left with wings level creates the illusion of the body tilted to the right [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

cards.s: The diving or rolling beyond the vertical plane demonstration usually gives the learner only a mild sense of climbing.
cards.why: False. It usually produces intense disorientation: a sense of falling downward into the direction of the roll [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

cards.s: In a steady turn, the fluid in the semicircular canals catches up with the canal walls within a second or two.
cards.why: False. It may take about 15 to 20 seconds, and after that the steady turn feels like no turn [[23:71|IFH 3-4]] [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

cards.s: Skids and slips can give the sensation of banking or tilting.
cards.why: True. The IFH lists skids and slips among the motions that mislead the inner ear [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

cards.s: Before flying in marginal visibility (less than 3 miles), the IFH says to get training and stay proficient in controlling the airplane by instruments.
cards.why: True. It is one of the IFH ways to cope with spatial disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

cards.s: Feeling nothing during a disorientation demo still teaches something.
cards.why: True. It shows the body cannot detect bank or roll [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

activities.title: A hood lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a CFI with a commercial applicant in a 110 knot trainer. Today: instrument turns to headings, then compass turns. The practice area is hazy but VFR.

steps.s: Before the hood goes on, what is the first thing to do in the air?
options: Calibrate the turn coordinator in both directions with the learner reading the clock
Start with a 180° compass turn to find the hardest part early
Have the learner fly steep turns to warm up the cross-check
Cover the attitude indicator so the learner trusts the turn coordinator
steps.why: Calibrate before timed and compass turns; 30° in 10 seconds is standard rate [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Building from simple to complex suits several skills at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

steps.s: On the first 90° turn the learner's eyes stay on the heading indicator and the altitude sags 120 feet. What do you do?
options: Take the controls at once and demonstrate the whole turn again
Point out the fixation, and coach a pitch check as the bank goes in and leaving the heading indicator alone for about 20 seconds
Tell them to watch the altimeter more closely for the rest of the turn
Cover the heading indicator for the rest of the lesson
steps.why: Fixation on a single bank instrument and preoccupation with bank on entry are listed errors; leave the heading indicator out about 20 seconds in a 90° turn and check pitch as bank starts [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

steps.s: You move on to turns steeper than standard rate. The learner's pitch control is late on every entry and altitude sags each time. What now?
options: Keep repeating the steep turns until the timing comes
Have them add a large power increase before each entry
Make the turn coordinator the primary pitch reference
Roll out, talk through the errors, and go back to shallower turns before steepening
steps.why: If pitch control is consistently late on steep entries, roll out to straight-and-level, analyze the errors, practice shallower turns, then increase the bank as the cross-check improves [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

steps.s: Turns are now consistent. How do you check whether the learner can still fly them under a realistic workload?
options: Remove the hood and have them fly the same turns visually
Give a task such as resetting the clock or finding a heading on a chart, then watch the next rollout
Cover the attitude indicator without telling them
Ask for faster roll-ins so each turn takes less time
steps.why: The AIH lists distractions such as resetting the clock and finding a heading to an airport on a chart [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Interruptions are where steps get skipped, so watch whether the rollout still starts at the lead point [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

steps.s: On the last turn the turn coordinator sits on the standard rate mark, but the ball is well off center. What do you coach?
options: Hold it; the turn coordinator is primary, so the ball does not matter
Recalibrate the turn coordinator before the next turn
Center the ball with rudder; until it is centered, do not assume the bank is making the turn
Roll wings level at once and start the turn again
steps.why: Failure to check the ball is a listed bank error: unless the ball is centered, do not assume the turn comes from a banked attitude [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Check the ball throughout the turn, especially if pressures are held [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
